results.evidence: Section 2.4: "During the Term and for eighteen (18) months after its expiration or termination, Distributor shall not, and shall cause its Affiliates not to, directly or indirectly, manufacture, purchase for resale, market, promote, distribute or sell any Competing Products anywhere in North America." Section 1.4: "'Competing Products' means any chemical used in the treatment of water or wastewater, whether or not it competes with the Products, other than Products purchased from Supplier under this Agreement."
results.reason: The problem is present and hurts Gloumund, the client. Read together, Sections 2.4 and 1.4 bar Gloumund and its Affiliates from selling any water-treatment chemical anywhere in North America. That covers non-competing items such as disinfectants. The bar runs for the Term plus 18 months. Yet the Products are only coagulants (Section 1.7), and Gloumund's exclusivity covers only NY, NJ and PA (Section 1.9). The restraint is far broader than any legitimate interest Droupourt could protect, which makes it vulnerable under New York's reasonableness test (BDO Seidman). Until it is narrowed or held unenforceable, it still restricts Gloumund's existing business. The prior draft (v2) limited the covenant to PAC/ferric sulfate coagulants in the Territory during the Term only. That shows the expansion was a change from the negotiated position, not an agreed benign term. The issue is live and actionable. Droupourt's March 16, 2026 letter invokes Section 2.4 against Gloumund's Connecticut sodium hypochlorite sales. It demands that Gloumund cease those sales and give a customer list, and it reserves termination and injunctive relief. Nothing in the folder shows Gloumund accepting the result or conceding.

results.evidence: Section 1.1: "'Products' means all products sold by Supplier or any of its Affiliates to Distributor or any of its Affiliates, together with all related packaging, totes, drums, deposits, freight and services." Section 1.3: "Terms defined in this Guaranty control for purposes of this Guaranty, notwithstanding any different definition in the Distribution Agreement."
results.reason: The problem is present and uncured. Distribution Agreement Section 1.7 limits 'Products' to the Exhibit A coagulants, and Section 16.1 calls only for a guaranty of 'Distributor's payment obligations'. The Guaranty instead defines Products, and so the Guaranteed Obligations in Section 1.2, to cover any sale by any Droupourt affiliate to any Gloumund affiliate, under the Distribution Agreement, 'any Purchase Order or otherwise'. Section 1.3 makes the Guaranty's definition prevail, and Distribution Agreement Section 18.4 says its order of precedence does not govern the Parent Guaranty, so nothing in the folder narrows it. Unrelated affiliate debts can therefore draw down the single $2,000,000 cap in Section 3. Only Guarantor payments restore nothing, so the cap stays reduced. That hurts the Gloumund group and the client directly: less credit support remains for the client's own purchases, and Guarantor holds subrogation rights against affiliates for those payments. If the parent later wants to escape the broader exposure by terminating under Section 9.2, that is expressly a breach of Section 16.1 by the client unless a replacement guaranty is delivered. The Guaranty can still be amended under Section 11.5, and nothing shows the group has accepted the broader scope, so the point remains actionable.

results.evidence: Section 12.3: "The limitations in Sections 12.1 and 12.2 apply to all liability under this Agreement, except for Distributor's obligations under Section 11.1." Section 11.1: Distributor shall indemnify Supplier "from and against all Claims and Losses, including environmental and regulatory Claims and Losses, arising out of or relating to the storage, handling, transport or resale of Products by or on behalf of Distributor, regardless of the cause."
results.reason: The problem is present and hurts the client. Distributor (Gloumund) gives the Section 11.1 indemnity. That indemnity applies "regardless of the cause", so it reaches losses caused by Supplier's own defective packaging, even though Section 6.2 makes Supplier responsible for tote integrity. Section 12.3 removes the cap and the consequential-damages exclusion only for Gloumund's indemnity. Supplier's reciprocal indemnity in Section 11.2 stays capped at 12 months of payments and has no environmental or packaging prong. The prior draft (v2) had a fault-based indemnity, a packaging carve-out, a mutual cap exclusion and comparative responsibility; all were removed in the signed agreement. Droupourt's March 16, 2026 letter tenders the NJDEP and Passaic Valley Sewerage Commission claim under Section 11.1 for a leaking Droupourt-filled tote. The folder shows no acceptance of the tender, no payment and no waiver by Gloumund. The exposure is therefore live and Gloumund can still act on it, for example by contesting scope, arguing the tote defect falls under Sections 6.2 and 8.1 or 11.2, or negotiating an amendment.
